content: An epidemic, as defined in the field of epidemiology, refers to the occurrence of new cases of a particular disease within a specific human population during a defined time period, at a rate that significantly exceeds what is typically expected based on recent historical data. The rate at which new cases appear in the population over a given time frame is referred to as the incidence rate. When this phenomenon occurs in animal populations, it is termed an epizootic. The classification of an epidemic can be somewhat subjective, as it depends on what is considered expected or normal for a given disease. An epidemic may be confined to a specific geographic area, in which case it is referred to as an outbreak. If it spreads more broadly, it is termed an epidemic, and if it becomes global in scale, it is classified as a pandemic. For example, even a small number of cases of a rare disease, such as rabies, may be labeled as an epidemic, whereas a large number of cases of a common illness, such as the common cold, would not typically be classified as such. Diseases that occur consistently at a relatively stable but high rate within a population are referred to as endemic diseases. Malaria in certain regions of Africa, such as Liberia, serves as an example of an endemic disease, as a significant proportion of the population is expected to contract malaria at some point during their lifetime. The term epidemic is not limited to infectious diseases and is often used to describe widespread societal issues that are increasing in prevalence. Examples include the epidemics of obesity, mental health disorders, and substance abuse. Historically, well-known examples of epidemics include the bubonic plague, also known as the Black Death, which devastated Medieval Europe, and the Great Influenza Pandemic that coincided with the conclusion of World War I. Several factors have been identified as contributors to the emergence of new epidemics. These include changes in agricultural practices and land use, shifts in societal structures and human demographics, poor population health (e.g., malnutrition or the presence of immunosuppressive conditions like HIV), the role of hospitals and medical procedures, the evolution of pathogens (e.g., increased virulence or resistance to antimicrobial drugs), contamination of water supplies and food sources, international travel, failures in public health programs, international trade, and climate change. Additional factors, as highlighted in reports by experts such as Professor Andy Dobson and Professor Akilesh Mishra, include reduced biodiversity due to environmental destruction and poor urban planning.g., meat, milk, and dairy products), prioritizing the consumption of locally sourced foods, eating crops that are in season, improving the efficiency of agricultural practices, avoiding the destruction of rainforests, and being willing to pay higher prices for meat. In August 2007, the World Health Organization (WHO) raised concerns about the unprecedented rate at which infectious diseases were spreading globally, highlighting the need for renewed vigilance and action to address this growing threat.
